opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest risk is that you end up building for a very unrepresentative slice of the world. Tech companies, especially the big Silicon Valley ones, have a lot of things most organizations don't. They have strong engineering teams, people who are comfortable stitching together open source components, and a tolerance for rough edges because they can work around them themselves. If those are your only customers, you can convince yourself a product is great when it really only works for people who could almost have built it themselves.

Most of the value of data and AI, though, is going to be realized in places like banks, hospitals, manufacturers, retailers, and government agencies. Those organizations have very different constraints. They care a lot about governance, security, compliance, and auditability. Their data is often messy and spread across legacy systems. And the people using the tools are usually analysts or domain experts, not infrastructure engineers. If you haven't designed for that from the start, it's very hard to retrofit later. Things like access control, lineage, and reliability end up as afterthoughts when they should be the foundation.

There's also a market risk. The set of tech-first companies is relatively small, and many of them will eventually build in-house rather than buy, because they have the talent and they see infrastructure as core to their business. So if that's your whole customer base, you're competing against your customers' own engineering teams, and you're quite exposed when budgets tighten.

Something we saw early on with Spark and later at Databricks is that the most interesting feedback often came from the less obvious users. A team at a pharmaceutical company or a utility would hit problems that no tech company ever would, and solving those made the product better for everyone. So I'd say you want a few sophisticated early adopters to push the technical frontier, but you really need to get into mainstream enterprises early so you understand what it takes to make the technology usable at scale by normal teams.

r001.rationale: The response explains that non-tech organizations have different needs and constraints, and says it is very hard to retrofit products for them if those needs were not addressed from the start.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, both from the Spark days and now at Databricks. The risk is basically that tech companies are the easiest customers and also the least representative ones. If you build for a Netflix or an Uber, you get these very sophisticated users who have big engineering teams, who will tolerate rough edges, who will read the source code if the docs are bad, and who already know what they want. So you get a lot of signal very quickly, and it feels like you're winning.

But that's maybe a few hundred companies in the world. The vast majority of the value from data and AI is going to be captured in industries like healthcare, manufacturing, financial services, retail, government, places that don't have a thousand engineers who grew up on Hadoop. And those customers have completely different constraints. They care about governance, about security, about not having to hire a specialized team just to keep the system running. They want something that works out of the box and that a data analyst or a domain expert can use, not just a distributed systems PhD.

If you only optimize for the tech crowd, you end up building a product that's extremely powerful and extremely hard to use, and you just don't notice because your early users never complained. We actually saw some of this with Spark early on. The API was great if you were a Scala programmer, and then we realized that most of the people who wanted to do this work were in Python or SQL, and the whole experience had to be rethought around them.

The other risk is more strategic. Tech companies will often build their own thing. They have the talent to do it, and they sometimes see infrastructure as a competitive advantage. So your most enthusiastic customers are also the ones most likely to churn by just reimplementing you internally, or by jumping to the next open source project. The customers in traditional industries are actually stickier, and they're the ones who need you to solve the whole problem rather than give them a toolkit.

So I'd say the discipline is to use the tech companies as a signal of where things are going, because they do tend to hit problems two or three years before everyone else, but to design the product for the much larger group of people who are going to encounter those same problems later with far fewer resources to deal with them.

r001.rationale: The response explains that optimizing for sophisticated tech-company users can produce a powerful but hard-to-use product that misses the needs and constraints of non-tech industries, making broader adoption harder.

astra-6.text: I think the risk is that tech companies aren’t representative of most customers. They have engineers who can integrate things, build tooling around your product, and figure out how to operate it. So you can get very positive feedback from them while building something that’s much too complicated for everyone else. You might also prioritize features that matter to a sophisticated infrastructure team, when another customer really just needs an easy way to solve a business problem. You have to talk to customers outside that bubble to understand what it takes for them to actually use the product.

r001.rationale: The response says tech customers can tolerate complexity because they have engineers, while the product may become too complicated for everyone else, making it harder for non-tech customers to use.

sol-6.1.text: I think the risk is that you overfit to a pretty unusual set of customers. Tech companies have a lot of engineers, they’re willing to assemble complicated systems, and they may even enjoy doing that. So you can build something that works really well for them but requires too much expertise for everyone else. You miss the opportunity to make the product simpler and useful to a much broader set of companies.

r001.rationale: It says the product may require too much expertise for everyone else and that this misses broader companies, clearly identifying a barrier to expanding beyond tech customers.
